As of 120 AM EST Monday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Warm conditions will prevail for another day, but a cold 
front will slide east today and bring cool breezy conditions behind 
it. The coastal system we've monitored the last several days is 
approaching eastern Massachusetts, and based on radar, we only 
have some virga to show for it. While this system lifts north-
north east, a cold front will shift east. The front will have 
marginal moisture, but perhaps could pick some off Lake Huron. 
Temperatures today will generally be in the 50s, though parts of
the Adirondacks and St. Lawrence Valley may observe a 
relatively early daytime high before steadily falling. A strong 
incoming surface high in the upper echelon of November MSLP 
values will filter in. The tightening pressure gradients will 
support widespread 20-30 mph gusts, locally up to 35 near 
Ellenburg, New York at the northeastern tip of the Adirondacks. 
Brisk 15-25 mph northwesterly gusts will continue overnight, 
which will help bring temperatures down into the 20s to near 30.

Our pattern will settle into cooler temperatures for a couple days 
with max temperatures in the 30s across the region on Tuesday. The 
surface high could peak around 1040-1042mb once its centered 
overhead Tuesday night. This will result in efficient radiational 
cooling. Most locations will fall into the teens to lower 20s, but 
thinking the Adirondack Airport could reach the single digits. 
Despite its strength, the strong surface high will make steady east 
progress, and this will bring south to southeast flow that will 
start deep, warm advection. As we approach the Thursday system, near 
to above freezing temperatures could span the lowest 5000-7000 ft of 
the atmosphere.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The forecast for Thanksgiving day and towards the 
weekend remains unchanged as a widespread rainfall event remains 
likely. Thermal profiles continue to support rain as the dominant 
precipitation type through much of the event. Given the positioning 
of the occluding upper low and the coastal low, colder air will be 
at a premium as Arctic air will remain largely locked north of the 
border. For us, this means a warmer system, with more widespread 
cold rain favored. Supporting this will be good warm moist air 
transport off the Atlantic by the coastal low. That said, as our 
strong high lifts to the northeast on Thanksgiving day, some cold 
air may linger at the onset in our climatologically favored 
locations in the NEK and northern St. Lawrence Valley (i.e. Essex 
County VT and near Massena, NY) before scouring out late Thursday. A 
brief period of wintry mix may be still be possible in the NEK and 
northern St. Lawrence Valley late Thanksgiving day, though impacts 
will be minimal due to the short duration of any wintry mix before 
transitioning to all rain overnight. Furthermore, soundings suggest 
that when temperatures would be supportive of any wintry mix at the 
onset, we will not be saturated enough at the surface to produce 
precipitation, and when we are saturated enough, temperatures will 
have warmed above freezing. Confidence in wintry weather continues 
to trend down. Rain will overspread the area late Thanksgiving Day 
into Friday when the period of steadiest precipitation is expected. 
Precipitation will turn more showery and become confined to the 
terrain as wrap around moisture, and westerly winds result in 
additional terrain driven valley rain and mountain snow showers into 
the weekend. However, moisture will be decreasing by Saturday and 
Sunday with little in the way of impacts expected over the weekend 
for post holiday travel. Last note on the precipitation side of 
things is that with the expected rainfall, there is no antecedent 
snowpack and with our recent relatively dry conditions, there are no 
significant hydro concerns for this event.

Aside from the precipitation aspect, the system will be carrying a 
rather strong jet with it as it tracks north Thursday night. NAEFS 
percentiles depict this associated jet as laying in the upper 
climate database into the 99th percentile at 850mb. Deterministic 
guidance points to a 65-75kt jet at 850mb (strongest across southern 
Vermont), which even with ongoing precipitation would bode some 
potential for gusty winds. We'll have to see how the hi-res guidance 
depicts the inversion layer when we get within the hi-res window, 
but it is reasonable that locations above 2000ft can expect gusty 
winds at least 25kt+ at this time Thursday night. These winds will 
be easterly, and with the strength of the 850mb layer, the direction 
would be favorable for downsloping winds, focused in the southern 
Greens of Rutland and southeastern Addison County. The question
